judgements.reason: UsageTemplate() returns the caller-supplied template when c.usageTemplate is non-empty and otherwise the default, whose second line emits the 'XXX [command]' entry guarded by {{if .HasAvailableSubCommands}}. The span contains both the exact bytes to be removed and the override condition.
The caller-facing procedure: SetUsageTemplate stores the replacement template into c.usageTemplate, which UsageTemplate() then returns in place of the default containing the '[command]' line.
The alternative override point; UsageFunc() is what renders UsageTemplate(), so replacing it also removes the line, but this span alone does not show the '[command]' bytes.

note: config_docs / how-mode. The pinned default usage template is the only place that produces the 'XXX [command]' line, and cobra exposes SetUsageTemplate (and SetUsageFunc) as the documented override, so the procedure is fully derivable from the pinned .go bytes.

judgements.reason: The caller procedure: SetHelpCommand assigns c.helpCommand, which is the field InitDefaultHelpCmd tests before creating cobra's built-in help command.

The controlling condition: the default help command is constructed only when c.helpCommand is nil (and only when the command has subcommands), so supplying one's own command through SetHelpCommand suppresses the default.
Explains why a replacement command marked Hidden (and not named 'help') disappears from the command listing: IsAvailableCommand returns false for hidden commands and for the parent's helpCommand.

note: config_docs / how-mode. Affirmative in-tree mechanism: call rootCmd.SetHelpCommand with a command of one's own (e.g. hidden) before Execute, because InitDefaultHelpCmd only builds cobra's help command when c.helpCommand is still nil. No option flag equivalent to CompletionOptions.DisableDefaultCmd exists for help at the pin, but the setter path is a positive, source-defined procedure.

D5, positive finding. The pinned tree states the ordering but never a cause. command.go:967-976 runs PreRunE/PreRun and only then calls c.ValidateRequiredFlags(); the ordering is bare code with no explanatory comment. ValidateRequiredFlags' doc comment (command.go:1146) says only 'validates all required flags are present and returns an error otherwise'. The Command lifecycle doc comment (command.go:114-122) enumerates PersistentPreRun/PreRun/Run/PostRun/PersistentPostRun and does not mention flag validation at all. A tree-wide grep for 'required flag' across tracked .go and .md files returns only command.go:1146 and 1165, flag_groups.go:54, completions.go:322/389/392/465 and site/content/user_guide.md:319 ('Required flags'), none of which give a rationale, and site/content/user_guide.md:605-614 documents the hook order without referencing validation. Answering the 'why' mode ('state the source-defined cause, condition, or invariant') would require synthesis the cited bytes do not support (e.g. inferring that hooks are allowed to set flag values before pflag.Changed is inspected); restating the ordering alone only restates the query.

judgements.anchor: // Use is the one-line usage message.
judgements.reason: The documentation unit for the Use field states that Use is the one-line usage message and gives the exact notation for writing arguments into it ([ ] optional, ... repeatable, | exclusive, { } required set), with the worked example 'add [-F file | -D dir]... [-f format] profile'. This is the mechanism by which arguments appear in usage text.

UseLine composes the printed usage line from the parent command path plus c.Use verbatim (appending ' [flags]' unless DisableFlagsInUseLine), showing that whatever argument text is placed in Use is what is rendered.
The default usage template consumes {{.UseLine}} under 'Usage:', connecting the Use field to the rendered usage text, but does not itself say how to write the arguments.

note: config_docs / how-mode. Affirmative answer at the pin: cobra does not synthesise argument names from Args/ValidArgs; the caller writes them into Command.Use, which UseLine renders into the {{.UseLine}} slot of the usage template.

judgements.anchor: Arguments that are not enclosed in brackets are required.
judgements.reason: The documenting half of the question: the Use field's recommended syntax states literally that bracketed arguments are optional and unbracketed arguments are required, and { } delimits a required mutually exclusive set. That is the source-defined convention for documenting a required argument.

The defining/enforcing half: MinimumNArgs returns a PositionalArgs validator that errors with 'requires at least %d arg(s)' when fewer args are supplied, i.e. how a required positional argument is enforced.
The exact-count variant of the same mechanism, erroring with 'accepts %d arg(s), received %d' when the required number of positional arguments is not present.
The field the validator is assigned to; ValidateArgs (command.go:1139-1144) calls it, but the field declaration alone does not state the procedure.

note: config_docs / how-mode, and Q has two alternatives ('document or define') that are both satisfied at the pin: document via the Use string convention, define/enforce via Command.Args with a PositionalArgs validator from args.go.

judgements.reason: The declared option asked about: SilenceErrors 'is an option to quiet errors down stream', with SilenceUsage alongside it for the usage block printed after an error.

The condition that makes it so: ExecuteC prints 'Error: <err>' via c.PrintErrln only when neither the executed command nor the root has SilenceErrors set, so setting it on the root suppresses the printed error entirely (Execute still returns the error).
The alternative in-tree lever: redirecting the error writer sends the same output elsewhere (e.g. io.Discard) rather than suppressing it; supports but does not alone answer the yes/no.

note: yes/no mode. Affirmative: yes, set SilenceErrors (and SilenceUsage) on the command, or redirect the error writer with SetErr; the printing site in ExecuteC shows the exact condition under which cobra emits the error text.

D5, positive finding. Related code exists but no span carries the requested procedure under either reading of 'order of different flags'. (a) Order in which flags were supplied on the command line: nothing in the pinned tree records it. ParseFlags (command.go:1818-1840) hands the raw argv straight to c.Flags().Parse(args) and keeps no positional record; stripFlags (command.go:643-678) and argsMinusFirstX (command.go:684-717) discard flag tokens rather than ordering them; the only ordering accessor on Command is ArgsLenAtDash (command.go:870-872), which is about the '--' position, not flag order. (b) Order in which flags are listed/visited: cobra only propagates pflag's SortFlags field (command.go:1679 'c.lflags.SortFlags = c.Flags().SortFlags', command.go:1861 'c.parentsPflags.SortFlags = false') and controls insertion order in mergePersistentFlags (command.go:1848-1854); the sorting/visiting semantics themselves are defined in github.com/spf13/pflag v1.0.5 (go.mod), which is not in the pinned tree. cobra.go:57-59 EnableCommandSorting orders commands, not flags. So there is no tracked .go span containing the value, condition or procedure asked for; nothing here is an effort or difficulty judgement.

D4, positive finding: the honest answer at the pin is only that cobra does not implement it. A tree-wide grep of tracked files for '@file', response/argument-file handling, and file reads during argument processing finds nothing; the single '@' hit in non-test .go source is bash_completions.go:281 (_filedir "@(${ext})", a bash extglob in a generated completion script, unrelated to argument expansion). Cobra's own token classification is exhaustive and has no '@' case: isFlagArg (command.go:719-721) recognises only '--x' and '-x' forms, and stripFlags (command.go:643-678) switches over '--', long flags, short flags and 'anything not starting with -' as a plain command/positional token. Argument parsing is then delegated wholesale to pflag via c.Flags().Parse(args) (command.go:1833). No affirmative answer exists, so A1 fails and absence must not be converted into a grade-3 span.

D4, positive finding. Hidden flags are unconditionally excluded from flag-name completion at the pin, with no opt-in. bash_completions.go:699-701 defines 'func nonCompletableFlag(flag *pflag.Flag) bool { return flag.Hidden || len(flag.Deprecated) > 0 }'. completions.go:534-537 makes getFlagNameCompletions return an empty slice for such a flag, and every path that suggests flag names goes through it: the general flag-name loop (completions.go:393-417) and completeRequireFlags (completions.go:567-590). The legacy bash generator applies the same guard at bash_completions.go:567, 581 and 597. CompletionOptions (completions.go:104-116) offers DisableDefaultCmd, DisableNoDescFlag, DisableDescriptions and HiddenDefaultCmd only - nothing to include hidden flags - and no annotation overrides nonCompletableFlag. The only 'answer' would be to stop hiding the flag, i.e. that cobra does not support completing hidden flags.

D4, positive finding. At the pin a subcommand can only be the first non-flag token, so commands preceded by variable positional arguments are not supported. Find/innerfind (command.go:726-748) computes argsWOflags := stripFlags(innerArgs, c) and tests only argsWOflags[0] against findNext; when findNext returns nil the recursion stops and the current command is returned (command.go:734-740), so 'app arg sub' resolves to 'app' with 'arg' as a positional. Traverse (command.go:790-829) behaves identically: the first token that is not a flag or a flag value is passed to c.findNext(arg), and 'if cmd == nil { return c, args, nil }'. findNext (command.go:767-786) matches only by name, alias or prefix at that single position. No field (TraverseChildren, DisableFlagParsing, Args, EnablePrefixMatching) changes which position is examined, and legacyArgs (args.go:24-39) then reports the leading token as 'unknown command'. Absence is the whole answer, so A1 fails.

judgements.reason: The mechanism that makes it possible: Flags() lazily creates and returns the command's live, mutable FlagSet, so a caller can register flags on it programmatically at any point (likewise PersistentFlags(), command.go:1725-1736) rather than only in a static init.

judgements.anchor: // do it here after merging all flags and just before parse
judgements.reason: The condition that fixes the deadline: ParseFlags calls mergePersistentFlags and only then c.Flags().Parse(args), so any flag added to the set before parsing (i.e. before Execute reaches this command) is picked up; flags added afterwards are not parsed.

judgements.anchor: at the last point possible to allow for user
judgements.reason: Cobra itself adds flags dynamically during execution at this point (InitDefaultHelpFlag/InitDefaultVersionFlag) and says why it defers them, corroborating that late registration before ParseFlags is the supported shape.

note: yes/no mode. Affirmative: yes - Flags()/PersistentFlags() expose the live FlagSet, and the source-defined condition is that registration must happen before ParseFlags runs for that command (execute() at command.go:888), which cobra itself relies on when it injects the help and version flags at execute time.

I could not settle which capability Q asks about, and the two readings give opposite verdicts, so I decline to guess. Reading A - literal single-dash multi-character option '-delete' (Go stdlib style): the pinned tree positively lacks it (isFlagArg, command.go:719-721, classifies '-delete' as a shorthand form; stripFlags, command.go:643-678, only treats a single-dash token as a value-taking flag when len(s)==2, i.e. a one-letter shorthand; all actual parsing is delegated to pflag at command.go:1833), which would be D4. Reading B - 'like git', i.e. a --delete option with a -d shorthand: the declaration API (BoolP/StringVarP and friends) belongs to github.com/spf13/pflag v1.0.5 (go.mod) and is absent from the pinned tree, cobra contributing only the Flags()/PersistentFlags() accessors, which would be D3. Both readings end in not_answerable but under different disqualifiers, and a third reading (a 'delete' subcommand in git's style, satisfied by AddCommand at command.go:1302-1329) would be answerable. Since the disqualifier and possibly the verdict depend on an intent I cannot fix from Q alone at the pin - and I am not permitted to read the issue body or comments - I report this as unresolved rather than pick one. This is not an effort or difficulty judgement.

judgements.reason: The core of the procedure, stated in the pinned source: SetArgs overrides the argv (otherwise os.Args[1:]) and its doc comment names testing as the purpose, so a test drives the CLI by setting the arguments on the root command and executing it.

The capture step: SetOut/SetErr redirect usage and error output to a caller-supplied writer (e.g. a bytes.Buffer) so a test can assert on the produced output; getOut/getErr (command.go:394-413) show the writers are inherited by children.
The invocation and assertion point: Execute runs the tree over the args and returns the error, with ExecuteC (command.go:1046-1136) additionally returning which command ran.

note: config_docs / how-mode. The ordered procedure is fully carried by pinned .go bytes: build/obtain the root command, SetArgs with the test argv, SetOut/SetErr to a buffer, call Execute (or ExecuteC for the executed command), assert on the returned error and buffered output. SetArgs' own doc comment at the pin names testing as its motivating use.

D3, positive finding: the necessary answer lives in a dependency repository, not the pinned tree. Uint64P is a method of pflag.FlagSet; cobra's Flags() simply returns *pflag.FlagSet (command.go:1641-1653) and go.mod pins github.com/spf13/pflag v1.0.5, whose source is not present at the pin. Whether Uint64P's value accepts hexadecimal, and how to make one that accepts decimal OR hex (a custom pflag.Value / SetValue), is defined entirely there. Grepping the pinned tree for Uint64, ParseUint or any numeric flag-value parsing returns nothing in cobra's own flag handling: the only strconv uses are cobra.go:124/135 (the 'gt' template helper) and doc/man_docs.go:128 (SOURCE_DATE_EPOCH). No tracked .go span in the pin contains the value, condition or procedure asked for.

judgements.reason: The discovery step: Commands() returns the command's child commands (sorted unless EnableCommandSorting is off), which is how a running program enumerates the subcommands it has registered.

The resolution step: Find walks the command tree for a given argument slice, matching the first non-flag token against the children with findNext and returning the target command plus its remaining args - the programmatic way to map arguments onto a discovered subcommand.

The registration step for subcommands built at runtime: AddCommand attaches children (and resets commandsAreSorted) at any point before Execute, so a dynamically discovered set of commands can be installed into the tree.

The dispatch step cobra itself performs: ExecuteC resolves the args with Traverse/Find and then runs cmd.execute(flags), showing the discover-then-execute sequence a caller reproduces via SetArgs + Execute.

note: config_docs / how-mode, read as: enumerate the subcommands of a command at run time and dispatch to one. All steps are carried by pinned .go bytes - AddCommand to register commands built at runtime, Commands() to enumerate, Find to resolve arguments to a target, Execute/ExecuteC to run it. Note that discovery of external plugin binaries as subcommands is not a cobra feature at the pin; this verdict rests on the in-process reading of the sealed question.

D4, positive finding, on the reading that 'argument' means a positional (non-flag) argument, which is cobra's own usage of the word (args.go PositionalArgs, stripFlags). At the pin the subcommand must be the first non-flag token, so nothing can be set before it. Find/innerfind (command.go:726-748) takes nextSubCmd := stripFlags(innerArgs, c)[0] and stops the descent when findNext returns nil; Traverse (command.go:790-829) likewise returns the current command as soon as a non-flag token fails findNext; legacyArgs (args.go:24-39) then reports that leading token as 'unknown command %q'. No field or option relocates that lookup position. Recorded ambiguity: if Q instead meant a flag before the subcommand, that is supported (stripFlags skips flag tokens at any position, and TraverseChildren at command.go:224-225 parses parent flags during traversal) and the row would be answerable; I judged the sealed wording 'argument' to mean a positional, and note the alternative here rather than silently rewriting the question.

D3, positive finding: the mechanism lives in the pflag dependency, absent from the pinned tree. Cobra defines no flag value types at all - it only hands out pflag's FlagSet (Flags(), command.go:1641-1653; PersistentFlags(), command.go:1725-1736) and calls c.Flags().Parse(args) (command.go:1833), with github.com/spf13/pflag v1.0.5 pinned in go.mod but not vendored. The single in-tree acknowledgement of multi-valued options is completions.go:393-399, which infers repeatability from strings.Contains(flag.Value.Type(), "Slice") / "Array" for the purpose of re-suggesting an already-used flag; it neither names a declaration API (StringSlice/StringArray/Var) nor states the syntax for supplying two values, so it is related-but-insufficient under A2 rather than answer-bearing. No tracked .go span at the pin contains the procedure asked for.

judgements.reason: The caller-facing switch: CompletionOptions.DisableDescriptions 'turns off all completion descriptions for shells that support them', set on the root command's CompletionOptions field (command.go:201-203).

The end-user route: InitDefaultCompletionCmd registers the '--no-descriptions' flag on each generated completion subcommand (bound to noDesc, which was seeded from CompletionOptions.DisableDescriptions at completions.go:711 and passed as !noDesc to GenBashCompletionV2 and its zsh/fish/powershell siblings).
The constants that give that flag its literal name, default and help text; supports the answer but does not by itself state the procedure.

The runtime effect: when the hidden completion command is invoked as __completeNoDesc, every completion is truncated at the tab that separates it from its description - the mechanism the generated no-description scripts rely on.

note: config_docs / how-mode. Two source-defined routes at the pin, both in .go bytes: set rootCmd.CompletionOptions.DisableDescriptions = true (which also suppresses the --no-descriptions flag via haveNoDescFlag at completions.go:695), or let the user pass '--no-descriptions' to the generated completion command; either way the script requests __completeNoDesc and descriptions after the tab are stripped.

judgements.anchor: initCompleteCmd adds a special hidden command
judgements.reason: The mechanism any external process can drive: every cobra program gets a hidden '__complete [command-line]' command (aliased __completeNoDesc, DisableFlagParsing, MinimumNArgs(1)) whose Run calls getCompletions on the arguments to complete - so a wrapper that os/exec's the binary obtains completions by executing it with __complete plus the words to complete.

The output contract the exec'ing caller must parse: one completion per line on stdout, then a final ':<directive>' line carrying the ShellCompDirective bitmap (stderr is informational and must be ignored, completions.go:249-251).
Names the two request commands (ShellCompRequestCmd '__complete' and ShellCompNoDescRequestCmd '__completeNoDesc') that the exec'd program responds to.

judgements.anchor: Only create this special command if it is actually being called.
judgements.reason: An essential condition for a program invoked by exec: the hidden command exists only for the invocation that actually calls it, so the completion request must be the first argument passed to the process and leaves no trace in normal runs.

note: config_docs / how-mode. Affirmative in-tree procedure: the exec'ing side runs the cobra binary as '<prog> __complete <args...> <toComplete>' (or __completeNoDesc for description-free output) and parses the completion lines plus the trailing ':<directive>' line; this is exactly what the generated shell scripts do (e.g. bash_completionsV2.go builds the same __complete invocation), so it is available to any caller that starts the CLI with os/exec.
